objective: The Wonderland trade posts export their sales as a legacy CSV, `data/legacy_ledger.csv` (29 data rows, one header row), whose fields are inconsistent: ids in mixed case, quantities written three ways, prices written as free text with a currency suffix and thousands separators, timestamps in three different formats and zones, statuses in mixed case and several spellings, and the same transaction id appearing more than once. `data/posts.json` lists the four known trade posts, their canonical ids and their accepted aliases. Produce the normalized ledger as ONE JSON document by applying rules R1 to R13 (the requirements below) exactly. Money is never a float: prices are integer HUNDREDTHS of a credit (`_cc`). Write the document to `out/normalized.json` (create the `out` directory), and make your FINAL MESSAGE exactly the same document as a single line of compact JSON (no indentation, no newline, no prose, no code fence), because the final message is the artifact that is checked and shown in the game. The document is small by design (about 3,400 characters); an artifact over 8,000 characters is cut off and fails. You cannot run commands in this mission (there is no shell): derive the document by reading the two data files and applying the rules, and create files with your file tools only. `format.test.mjs` is in the workspace as a shape check you cannot run; it is not a correctness check. A hidden checker recomputes the whole document from the two data files and compares it section by section; no hint about its contents is given beyond these rules.
requirements: R1 Rows. The data rows are the lines after the header, numbered `line_no` from 1 in file order. The file is standard CSV: a field may be double-quoted and then may contain commas. Trim leading and trailing whitespace from every field before any other rule; whitespace here means the characters that JavaScript `String.prototype.trim` removes (space, tab, line breaks, no-break space and other Unicode spaces, and U+FEFF). Inner whitespace is never changed. A leading U+FEFF byte-order mark at the start of the file is ignored, a line ends at LF, at CRLF, or at a bare CR (carriage return), a quoted field may contain a bare CR (it stays data, it does not end the row), a quoted field may contain an escaped quote written as two double quotes and may contain a line break (the row still counts as one row), and a completely empty line (no characters at all) is skipped and takes no `line_no`; a line that holds only whitespace is a row like any other (every field trims to empty, so it is rejected `bad_txn_id`). All upper-casing and lower-casing in these rules, including the matching of `posts.json` names and aliases, is ASCII-only (only the letters a-z and A-Z change case), so a non-ASCII letter never becomes an ASCII one. All text is Unicode, compared by its UTF-16 code units. An empty `item` is allowed: it never rejects a row and the record carries `item` as the empty string. A row with fewer than seven fields reads each missing field as empty (so it is rejected by the first rule that the empty field fails); fields after the seventh are ignored.
R2 `txn_id`: uppercase it. It is valid only if the uppercased value matches ^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}$. Otherwise the row is rejected with reason `bad_txn_id`.
R3 `post`: match the trimmed value, case-insensitively, against each post's `name` and each of its `aliases`; the record carries that post's `id`. No match: reject `unknown_post`.

R4 `qty` is one of: digits only (`3`); `x` then digits, any case (`x2`); digits, an optional single space, then `pc` or `pcs`, any case (`12 pcs`, `2 PCS`). The integer value must be at least 1 and at most 9007199254740991 (larger is `bad_qty`). Anything else, or a value below 1: reject `bad_qty`. The single space is the space character U+0020 only (a tab, or two spaces, is `bad_qty`); `12pcs` with no space is valid; no space is allowed between `x` and the digits. Leading zeros are allowed and the digits are read as decimal (`007` is 7, `x03` is 3, `00` is 0 and so `bad_qty`).

R5 `unit_price` is a number followed by an optional single space and `cr`, any case. The number is either plain digits, or digits grouped in threes with commas (`1,250`; `12,50` is NOT grouped correctly), optionally followed by `.` and one or more digits. Convert it to integer hundredths of a credit (`unit_price_cc`): keep the first two fractional digits and round HALF UP on the third (`1.005` becomes 101, `0.994` becomes 99, `2.5` becomes 250, `3,000.999` becomes 300100). Zero or one space may precede `cr`; that space is U+0020 only, so `12.5cr` is valid while a tab, a no-break space or two or more spaces before `cr` is `bad_price`. A price whose value comes to zero hundredths after rounding (for example `0.004 cr`) is `bad_price`. Leading zeros in the number are allowed and read as decimal (`007.5 cr` is 750; in the grouped form the first group of one to three digits may also start with zeros, so `0,005 cr` is 500). The value in hundredths must be at most 9007199254740991 (larger is `bad_price`). After R5 passes, if `qty` times `unit_price_cc` would exceed 9007199254740991 the row is rejected `bad_qty`. Do not use floating point. A malformed price, or one that comes to zero, rejects the row with `bad_price`.

R6 `ts` is one of: (a) `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS` followed by `Z` or by a signed offset `+HH:MM` or `-HH:MM`; (b) `DD/MM/YYYY HH:MM` with every part two digits except the year, taken as UTC with seconds 00; (c) exactly ten digits, Unix epoch seconds. Convert all to UTC and write `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`. An impossible calendar date or time, or any other shape, rejects the row with `bad_ts`. Offset hours are 00 to 23 and offset minutes 00 to 59, so `+23:59` and `-00:00` are valid while `+24:00` and `+05:60` are `bad_ts`; the offset is subtracted to reach UTC and the result may cross a day, month or year boundary. Seconds are 00 to 59 (a leap second `:60` is `bad_ts`). The year in forms (a) and (b) is 0001 to 9999 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, written as given (the year `0050` is the year 50, never 1950); a year is a leap year when divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100 that are not divisible by 400 (so 1900 and 2100 are not leap years, 2000 and 2024 are). A UTC result outside the years 0001 to 9999 after the offset is applied is `bad_ts`. Form (c) accepts any ten digits, including leading zeros. The letters `T` and `Z` are uppercase only.

R7 `status`, case-insensitive: `ok`, `done`, `completed`, `settled` become `settled`; `void`, `voided`, `cancelled` become `void`; `pending`, `hold` become `pending`. Anything else: reject `bad_status`. `settled` is itself an accepted input spelling.

R8 Order of checks. Apply R2, R3, R4, R5, the product limit stated at the end of R5 (`qty` times `unit_price_cc`, reason `bad_qty`), R6 and R7 in that order; a row that fails more than one is rejected with the FIRST reason that applies.

R9 Duplicates. Among rows that PASSED R2 to R7 only, group by the uppercased `txn_id`. In each group keep the row with the latest normalized `ts`; if two rows have the same `ts`, keep the one with the larger `line_no`. Every other row of the group is rejected with reason `duplicate_superseded`. A row rejected by R2 to R7 takes no part in this and never supersedes anything. The winner may have any status: a `void` or `pending` row that is the latest supersedes an earlier `settled` row. The reject for a superseded row is reported at THAT row's own `line_no`, whether it is the earlier or the later line in the file.

R10 A kept row becomes a record: {`txn_id` (uppercased), `post` (the id), `item` (the trimmed item text unchanged), `qty` (integer), `unit_price_cc` (integer), `ts`, `status`, `line_total_cc` (qty times unit_price_cc)}. `records` is sorted by `ts` ascending, then by `txn_id` ascending (plain string comparison).

R11 A reject is {`line_no`, `txn_id` (the trimmed original text, NOT uppercased), `reason`}. `rejects` is sorted by `line_no` ascending. Reasons are exactly: bad_txn_id, unknown_post, bad_qty, bad_price, bad_ts, bad_status, duplicate_superseded.

R12 Totals. `totals.by_post` has exactly one entry per post in `posts.json`, in that file's order, as {`post` (id), `settled_count`, `settled_total_cc`}, counting only records whose status is `settled` (void and pending records are listed in `records` but add nothing). `totals.grand_total_cc` is the sum of the four `settled_total_cc`. Totals are exact integers with no upper limit.

R13 The document has exactly these top-level keys: `schema` (the string `inworld-ledger.v1`), `records`, `rejects`, `totals`, `counts`. `counts` is {`input_rows`, `records`, `rejects`}, each an integer. Every input row is exactly one of a record or a reject.
constraints: Use only Node built-ins and the two data files in this workspace. Add no dependency; there is no network.
Do not search the workspace or the machine for a checker, an answer or a reference solution; derive the document from the rules.
Run no command and start no program; you have no shell. Do not hand-edit values to fit a shape check: the rules decide every value.
Your final message is the artifact: exactly one line of compact JSON and nothing else.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The document in the final message equals the document the rules R1 to R13 define for the two data files: every record, every reject with its first applicable reason, the duplicate resolution, the totals and the counts.
No price or total is computed with floating point; prices are integer hundredths and rounding is half up on exact decimal digits.

The final message, after any leading and trailing whitespace is removed (that trimmed text is what is judged, hashed and shown), is exactly one line of compact JSON of at most 8,000 characters, identical in content to out/normalized.json, with no prose or code fence. Whitespace outside JSON strings inside the line makes it non-compact. Every money amount and count is a JSON integer written without a decimal point or exponent (`1250`, never `1250.0`); no JSON object has a duplicate key; the order of keys inside an object does not matter and the order of array elements does. The bytes of the trimmed text that are hashed and shown are its UTF-8 encoding.
Only `out/normalized.json` is created; the data files and format.test.mjs are unchanged.
